newsitem.title: USA: Emerging market debts dip with U.S. Treasuries.
newsitem.headline: Emerging market debts dip with U.S. Treasuries.

text.p: Falling U.S. Treasuries in late afternoon trading knocked emerging market debts mostly lower, traders said.
The unexpected volatility was unnerving, a trader said.
"We have (had) big swings for three days," the trader said. "It makes you wonder..."

While most emerging market players still expect the Federal Reserve to keep credit policy unchanged at next week's Open Market Committee Meeting, caution was the byword, he said. He also noted that floaters were doing better than fixed rate bonds.
Ecuador debt continued its slide as player shunned high yielders. Ecuador PDI lost 1.00 to 66-1/8 bid.
Traders were trying to get a reading of sentiment shift in trading patterns, but so far to no avail.
Argentina FRB fell on Tuesday after a big block was unloaded in the market, a trader said.
Speculation that the seller was about to buy back some of the bonds pushed prices higher early in the day, but the buying apparently failed to materialize, he said.
FRB was bid 1/8 lower at 3-7/8.
Argentina's President Menem is expected to make changes of replacing the interior and the justice minister as well as ministers with portfolios in health and social services.

The changes could signal the start of a difficult period in politics prior to the key mid-term election on October 26, although the impact on the conduct of the economic policy would be minimal, said Jaime Valdivia, a vice president in emerging markets research at Morgan Stanley, Dean Witter, Discovery & Co.
"The third quarter could be difficult for Argentina," he said.

Faced with widespread social protest against the austerity program, the government is under pressure to increase spending and create news jobs, Valdivia said, who forecast that the fiscal account deficit in the third quarter would widen to 2.0 percent of the gross domestic product from an earlier estimate of 1.5 percent.

The wafer-thin slim majority of the ruling Peronist party does not give President Menem much maneuvering room, which makes the Argentine election more unpredictable than the Mexican election, Valdivia said.

But in Mexico, if the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party indeed loses its majority in Congress after being in power since 1929, a knee-jerk reaction could trigger some selling from surprised investors, he said.
Stronger economic fundamentals in Mexico vis-a-vis Argentina would argue a switch, but Valdivia advised investors to wait until the fallout of the Mexican elections was over before making the move.
Mexico's UMS-26 global bond was off 1/2 at 114-1/4 bid.
Among the Latin assets, Venezuela managed to edge higher on hopes of Brady debt restructuring deals, traders said.
Venezuela FLIRBs VZ6C97=RR added 3/8 to 93-1/8 bid.
